$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u={y}^{2}-2\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=2y, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}={e}^{2y-1}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y=\int {e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y=\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({y}^{2}-2){e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =({y}^{2}-2)(\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2})-\int (\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2})(2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{({y}^{2}-2){e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\int y\,{e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int y\,{e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=y\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}={e}^{2y-1}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y=\int {e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y=\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,{e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =(y)(\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2})-\int (\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2})(1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{y\,{e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{y\,{e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{4}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({y}^{2}-2){e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y & =\frac{({y}^{2}-2){e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\int y\,{e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{({y}^{2}-2){e}^{2y-1}}{2}-(\frac{y\,{e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{4}+D) \\  & =\frac{({y}^{2}-2){e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\frac{y\,{e}^{2y-1}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{4}-D \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{4}(2{y}^{2}-2y-3)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-D.$ 

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}-2){e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y & ={[\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{4}(2{y}^{2}-2y-3)]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{2(2)-1}}{4}(2(2)^{2}-2(2)-3))-(\frac{{e}^{2(0)-1}}{4}(2(0)^{2}-2(0)-3)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{4}(8-4-3)-\frac{1}{4e}(0-0-3) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{4}+\frac{3}{4e} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{4}+3}{4e}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e23dfcde-ad81-55af-adf6-6a05704da2aa"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e23dfcde-ad81-55af-adf6-6a05704da2aa" :answer-field/id #uuid "e23dfcde-ad81-55af-adf6-6a05704da2aa" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-ae03c0d2-b48d-57a5-8cfb-d6756b8b3bf3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ae03c0d2-b48d-57a5-8cfb-d6756b8b3bf3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ae03c0d2-b48d-57a5-8cfb-d6756b8b3bf3" :answer/id #uuid "ae03c0d2-b48d-57a5-8cfb-d6756b8b3bf3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{e^4+3}{4e}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-b249bd56-a311-5aac-8127-3bb428050e53" :question/id #uuid "b249bd56-a311-5aac-8127-3bb428050e53" :question/math-academy-id "q-12702" :question/problem "Calculate the integral of $\int 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "We need to use integration by parts.

We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={t}^{2}+1\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2t, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{2t+1}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t=\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =({t}^{2}+1)(\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2})-\int (\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2})(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\int t\,{e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\displaystyle\int t\,e^{2t+1}\,\textrm{d}t.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{2t+1}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t=\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t\,{e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t)(\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2})-\int (\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2})(1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{t\,{e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{t\,{e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{4}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\int t\,{e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}}{2}-(\frac{t\,{e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{4}+D) \\  & =\frac{({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\frac{t\,{e}^{2t+1}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{4}-D \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{4}(2{t}^{2}-2t+3)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C = -{D}.$

$$

$$

Using the formula for integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =({x}^{2})(\frac{1}{3}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))-\int (\frac{1}{3}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\frac{2}{3}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\displaystyle \int x\sin(3x) \textrm{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) & \,⟹\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\text{d}x=-\,\frac{1}{3}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,.\end{aligned}
$$

[{:db/id 17592186069905 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070031 :tutorial/content "We know that we can use the method of integration by parts to evaluate $\displaystyle \int xe^{4x} \textrm{d}x.$ Now, Let's  try. We define $u$ and $v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={e}^{4x} & \,⟹\,v=\int {e}^{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So the formula for integration by parts leads to

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{e}^{4x}\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}(\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})-\int (\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{2}\int x{e}^{4x}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We still don't have an answer, but the problem is reduced to the calculation of a simpler integral  $\displaystyle \int xe^{4x} \textrm{d}x.$ To compute this integral, we just need to apply the integration by parts formula again. For this second integral, we take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={e}^{4x} & \,⟹\,v=\int {e}^{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x}\,.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

where $C_1$ is a constant of integration.
So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{e}^{4x}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{2}\int x{e}^{4x}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{4}\,x{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{16}\,{e}^{4x}+{C}_{1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{8}\,x{e}^{4x}+\frac{1}{32}\,{e}^{4x}-\frac{{C}_{1}}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{32}\,{e}^{4x}(8{x}^{2}-4x+1)+C\end{aligned}
$$
